power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background | Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is a common cause of ischemic symptoms in patients with angina and non-obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA), predominantly women.
Neutrophils may contribute to CMD via vascular inflammation and endothelial injury.
We therefore investigated neutrophil and coronary endothelial cells in women with ANOCA.
In this cross-sectional study, we collected blood samples from ANOCA patients (n=123, 84% women) undergoing coronary function testing.
Complete blood counts (CELL-DYN, n=123) and neutrophil activation (AQUIOS, n=76) were assessed.
Isolated neutrophils were profiled using single-cell RNA-seq (n=11).
Guidewirederived coronary endothelial cells (n=7) isolated during coronary function testing were cultured to passage 2 for bulk RNA-seq.
Results | Of 103 women with ANOCA, 23 (22%) were diagnosed with CMD (CFR<2.5).
text.formatted: Results | Of 103 women with ANOCA, 23 (22%) were diagnosed with CMD (CFR<2.5).

text.text: These women showed higher NT-proBNP than women without CMD (234 [136-416] pg/ml vs. 112 [79-200] pg/ml, p<0.001).
text.formatted: These women showed higher NT-proBNP than women without CMD (234 [136-416] pg/ml vs. 112 [79-200] pg/ml, p<0.001).

text.text: Neutrophil counts, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and systemic immune-inflammation index were higher among women with a lower coronary flow reserve (CFR).
The proportion of activated neutrophils (CD62L dim ) was inversely associated with CFR at baseline.
Single-cell RNA-seq identified four neutrophil clusters, including interferon (IFN)-activated and immature neutrophils.
The IFN-activated cluster was expanded in patients with lower CFR and its proportion was inversely associated with surface CD62L expression.
Immature neutrophils showed reduced translational and increased inflammatory gene expression in patients with low CFR.
Coronary endothelial cells from patients with increased CD62L dim neutrophils showed higher proliferative/metabolic and lower IFN, complement and coagulation pathway activity.
Conclusion | Reduced CFR in women with ANOCA is associated with neutrophil activation, expansion of an IFNactivated neutrophil population, and altered immature neutrophil transcriptional programs.
Neutrophil activation is accompanied by distinct endothelial signatures.
These findings implicate neutrophil-endothelial interactions in CMD and identify IFN-associated neutrophil states as targets for mechanistic investigation.
Angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA) is a highly prevalent yet clinically challenging condition among patients undergoing coronary angiography, particularly among women 1, 2 .

text.text: A central mechanism underlying ANOCA is coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), which is characterized by impaired regulation of coronary microvascular function, resulting in an inadequate increase in myocardial blood supply in response to myocardial demand 3 .

text.text: Importantly, CMD is associated with high angina burden and adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including an increased risk of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction 4, 5 .

text.text: Despite this burden, effective and mechanism-guided treatments remain limited 6, 7 .

text.text: Elucidating the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms is therefore crucial to identify potential therapeutic targets and improve the management of patients with CMD.
Although the mechanisms underlying CMD remain incompletely understood, both coronary endothelial dysfunction and systemic low-grade inflammation have been implicated in its pathophysiology 8, 9 .

text.text: For instance, circulating IL-6 and TNF- have been associated with reduced coronary flow reserve (CFR) in obese patients without clinical heart disease 10 .

text.text: In addition, microvascular diseases are highly prevalent in chronic inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus [11] [12] [13] [14] , both of which disproportionately affect women.

text.text: Within these diseases, neutrophils play a central role [15] [16] [17] .

text.text: They are key effector cells of the innate immune system and may link systemic inflammation to coronary microvascular impairment, as hypothesized previously in ANOCA 18 .

text.text: Upon activation, neutrophils adhere to the endothelium and release reactive oxygen species, proteases, and inflammatory mediators, which can disrupt the endothelial barrier and impair nitric oxide mediated vasodilation.
Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) may further contribute to endothelial injury by promoting endothelial activation, inducing oxidative stress and creating a prothrombotic environment 19, 20 .

text.text: Beyond their established role in inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, neutrophil activation has also been implicated in coronary plaque erosion 21 , a pathology that is also characterized by sex-differences 22 .

text.text: These mechanisms provide a biological rationale for investigating the role of neutrophils in CMD.

Given the involvement of neutrophils in several female-predominant diseases, we investigated neutrophil abundance, activation and transcriptional states, together with coronary endothelial cell transcriptional profiles, in relation to CMD and invasively measured CFR in women with ANOCA.
Blood sampling and isolation of coronary-catheterization derived endothelial cells was performed at the University Medical Center Utrecht as part of the ENDOTYPE biobank (TCbio 24-203).
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the coronary function test.

Participation in the Netherlands Registry of Invasive Coronary Vasomotor Function Testing (NL-CFT, 21-473) 23 was a prerequisite for inclusion in the ENDOTYPE biobank, which enabled linkage of the biological samples to the corresponding clinical and procedural data.

All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

For the present study, patients with obstructive coronary artery disease, as identified prior to the coronary function test and patients with incomplete CFR measurements were excluded.

After exclusion of functionally significant epicardial coronary artery disease (non-hyperemic pressure ratio >0.89 or fractional flow reserve >0.80), ANOCA patients underwent invasive coronary function testing in the left anterior descending artery, including vasospasm provocation testing and coronary vasodilatory capacity assessment.

text.text: The procedure has been described in detail previously 24 .
text.formatted: The procedure has been described in detail previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Intracoronary acetylcholine provocation testing was used to assess coronary vasospasm, using incremental acetylcholine doses of 20, 100 and 200mg.

Spasm diagnosis was based on the Coronary Vasomotor Disorders International Study Group criteria 25 : epicardial spasm required reproducible angina, ischemic electrocardiographic changes, and >90% epicardial vasoconstriction; microvascular spasm required recognizable anginal symptoms and ischemic electrocardiographic changes without >90% epicardial vasoconstriction.
text.formatted: Spasm diagnosis was based on the Coronary Vasomotor Disorders International Study Group criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> : epicardial spasm required reproducible angina, ischemic electrocardiographic changes, and >90% epicardial vasoconstriction; microvascular spasm required recognizable anginal symptoms and ischemic electrocardiographic changes without >90% epicardial vasoconstriction.

text.text: Tests with symptoms or ischemic electrocardiographic changes alone were considered inconclusive (or equivocal).

Coronary vasodilatory capacity was assessed using continuous thermodilution, using a pressure-and temperature-sensitive sensor equipped guidewire (PressureWire X, Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, USA) together with a RayFlow infusion catheter (Hexacath, Paris, France) positioned in the proximal left anterior descending artery, as described previously 24 .
text.formatted: Coronary vasodilatory capacity was assessed using continuous thermodilution, using a pressure-and temperature-sensitive sensor equipped guidewire (PressureWire X, Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, USA) together with a RayFlow infusion catheter (Hexacath, Paris, France) positioned in the proximal left anterior descending artery, as described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Absolute coronary blood flow was quantified under resting and hyperemic conditions during saline infusion at 10 and 20 mL/min, respectively.
Measurements were obtained using dedicated software (CoroVentis, Uppsala, Sweden) based on the continuous thermodilution principle.
Absolute microvascular resistance was calculated as distal coronary pressure divided by absolute coronary blood flow.
Coronary flow reserve (CFR) was defined as the ratio of hyperemic to resting absolute coronary blood flow and microvascular resistance reserve was calculated as previously described 26 .
text.formatted: Coronary flow reserve (CFR) was defined as the ratio of hyperemic to resting absolute coronary blood flow and microvascular resistance reserve was calculated as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: For the present study, a diagnosis of CMD was defined as an absolute CFR <2.5, consistent with established diagnostic thresholds for impaired vasodilatory capacity 27.
text.formatted: For the present study, a diagnosis of CMD was defined as an absolute CFR <2.5, consistent with established diagnostic thresholds for impaired vasodilatory capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref>.

text.text: Blood samples were collected from ANOCA patients during the coronary function test, before any intracoronary measurements were performed.
First, systemic blood samples were obtained from the radial or femoral arterial sheath immediately after vascular access was established.
Second, local blood samples were collected from the guiding catheter after engagement of the left anterior descending artery.
Both blood samples were collected following heparin administration to minimize procedural influences.

Clinical biomarkers, including total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, creatinine and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), were measured retrospectively in plasma samples obtained from systemically collected EDTA-anticoagulated blood.
Blood samples were centrifuged at 1,850g for 10 minutes at room temperature with brake (Hettich centrifuge).
Afterwards, the plasma was stored at -80°C and was thawed once before clinical biomarker measurements.

Total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides and creatinine were measured using the Atellica CI analyzer (Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Germany) and NT-proBNP was measured using the Atellica IM immunoassay analyzer (Siemens Healthineers).
Lipid parameters and creatinine were quantified using enzymatic assays with photometric detection.
NT-proBNP was quantified using a fully automated, two-site sandwich immunoassay based on direct chemiluminescence.

Hematological complete blood cell counts were routinely measured in systemic and local EDTAanticoagulated blood samples using the CELL-DYN Sapphire hematology analyzer (Abbott Diagnostics, Abbott Park, IL, USA).
Available measurements for all included patients were retrieved from the Utrecht Patient Orientated Database (UPOD) 28 .
text.formatted: Available measurements for all included patients were retrieved from the Utrecht Patient Orientated Database (UPOD) <ref type="bibr">28</ref> .

text.text: Parameters included red blood cell indices (hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration and red cell distribution width), platelet count, total leukocyte count, and differential leukocyte counts (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils).
The neutrophil-tolymphocyte ratio (NLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII, platelet x neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio) were calculated from absolute counts.
Immediately after collection, systemic and local blood samples collected in sodium-heparin tubes, were loaded onto the AQUIOS CL 'Load & Go' flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Miami, FL, USA) 29 .
text.formatted: Immediately after collection, systemic and local blood samples collected in sodium-heparin tubes, were loaded onto the AQUIOS CL 'Load & Go' flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Miami, FL, USA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">29</ref> .

text.text: This platform fully automates sample preparation and flow cytometric analysis, including sample mixing, pipetting and staining with antibodies.
After a 15-minute incubation, red blood cells were lysed by adding 335 ml of lysing reagent A. Next, 100 ml of lysing reagent B was added to stop the lysis and preserve leukocyte integrity.
The prepared samples were then aspirated for analysis.
Absolute leukocyte counts were determined by electronic volume measurement.

To assess neutrophil surface marker expression, a custom antibody panel was used, consisting of CD64-PC7 (clone 22, Beckman Coulter, Miami, FL, USA), CD16-FITC (clone 3G8, Beckman Coulter), CD11b-PE (clone Bear1, Beckman Coulter), CD62L-ECD (clone DREG56, Beckman Coulter) and CD10-PC5 (clone ALB1, Beckman Coulter).

To assess neutrophil responsiveness, each sample was measured both unstimulated and after stimulation with the bacterial/mitochondrial-derived stimulus Nformyl-norleucyl-leucyl-phenalalanine (fNLF, BioCat GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany) at a final concentration of 10 -5 M. fNLF is a bacterial formyl-peptide receptor agonist that stimulates neutrophil activation, including degranulation and the mobilization of adhesion molecules 30.
text.formatted: To assess neutrophil responsiveness, each sample was measured both unstimulated and after stimulation with the bacterial/mitochondrial-derived stimulus Nformyl-norleucyl-leucyl-phenalalanine (fNLF, BioCat GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany) at a final concentration of 10 -5 M. fNLF is a bacterial formyl-peptide receptor agonist that stimulates neutrophil activation, including degranulation and the mobilization of adhesion molecules <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">30</ref>.

text.text: For detailed analysis, data files were exported from the AQUIOS CL flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software (Tree Star Inc.
Ashland, OR, USA).
Granulocytes were gated based on forward and side scatter, followed by neutrophil identification based on CD16 and CD11b co-expression.
The number of cells/L was calculated by multiplying the gated events with a correction factor of 232558.139535.
The median fluorescent intensity (MFI) of the different markers was determined within this neutrophil gate.
Neutrophil phenotypes were classified by quadrant gating based on CD16 and CD62L expression, as previously described 31 .
text.formatted: Neutrophil phenotypes were classified by quadrant gating based on CD16 and CD62L expression, as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">31</ref> .

text.text: The gating strategy for CD16/CD62L-based phenotyping is shown in Supplemental Figure S1.
text.formatted: The gating strategy for CD16/CD62L-based phenotyping is shown in Supplemental Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>.

text.text: Immediately after blood collection, polymorphonuclear neutrophils were isolated by layering of EDTAanticoagulated systemic whole blood onto of Polymorph prep™ (Axis-Shield, CAT#1114683; 1:1 v/v), followed by immediate centrifugation at 500g for 35 min at room temperature, as described in detail before 21 .
text.formatted: Immediately after blood collection, polymorphonuclear neutrophils were isolated by layering of EDTAanticoagulated systemic whole blood onto of Polymorph prep™ (Axis-Shield, CAT#1114683; 1:1 v/v), followed by immediate centrifugation at 500g for 35 min at room temperature, as described in detail before <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Leftover red blood cells were removed via hypotonic lysis using 10 mL of ice-cold dH₂O for 10-30 seconds, immediately neutralized with 10 mL of 2xPBS (Sigma Aldrich, CAT#D8537), and centrifuged at 400g for 5 minutes at 4°C. For single-cell RNA sequencing, a 100 μL aliquot of the purified PMN suspension (diluted with 1x PBS to 3.5 × 10⁵ cells/mL) was processed according to the GEXSCOPE Single-Cell RNA Library for NEO Handbook 32.

The library concentration and fragment size distribution were assessed using a Qubit High Sensitivity dsDNA kit on a Qubit 4 fluorometer (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and the TapeStation High Sensitivity D1000 tape (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA).

The libraries were pooled in an equimolar fashion and sent to GeneWiz (Azenta Life Sciences, Leipzig, Germany) to be sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X to an average depth of 30,000 reads/cell in a 2x150 bp manner.
The BCL files were demultiplexed to fastq files on Illumina's BaseSpace platform.
Libraries were excluded from downstream analysis when sequencing quality control indicated a low median UMI count per cell, consistent with low sample or cDNA quality.
Raw sequencing fastq files were processed into gene expression matrices using CeleScope™ version 2.11.3 (Singleron Biotechnologies, Cologne, Germany, https://github.com/singleron-RD/CeleScope).
text.formatted: Raw sequencing fastq files were processed into gene expression matrices using CeleScope™ version 2.11.3 (Singleron Biotechnologies, Cologne, Germany, <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/singleron-RD/CeleScope">https://github.com/singleron-RD/CeleScope</ref>).

text.text: Fastq file barcode chemistry determination and barcode correction were performed before being demultiplexed and gene counts generated using the STARSolo single-cell pipeline with STAR version 2.7.11a.
The human reference genome (GRCh38) was used for mapping the reads and annotation was done with Ensembl version 99.
Cell calling was based on bimodal modeling using the EmptyDrops algorithm.

Samples were additionally excluded from downstream analysis if their gene-barcode matrices were dominated by near-empty droplets, with the majority of nominally called cells failing minimum UMI/gene-count thresholds upon reanalysis.

Doublet detection and standard per-cell quality-control filtering (based on library size, gene number and mitochondrial and hemoglobin content) were performed per sample prior to merging the individual patient libraries into a single dataset for downstream integration.
Non-neutrophil populations were excluded based on marker gene expression.
Data were normalized using SCTransform (glmGamPoi), followed by principal component analysis (30 PCs), batch correction using Harmony, and shared nearest-neighbor clustering.
A clustering resolution of 0.1, yielding four clusters, was selected based on mean silhouette width.

Clusters were annotated using canonical markers, differential gene expression analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; log2 fold change threshold 0.25) and pathway enrichment (clusterProfiler; GO Biological Process).

To assess concordance with an independent human neutrophil reference atlas, per-cluster module scores were calculated (AddModuleScore, Seurat) using neutrophilspecific gene signatures derived from a large single-cell atlas of human neutrophils 33.
text.formatted: To assess concordance with an independent human neutrophil reference atlas, per-cluster module scores were calculated (AddModuleScore, Seurat) using neutrophilspecific gene signatures derived from a large single-cell atlas of human neutrophils <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref>.

text.text: Transcriptional relationships among clusters were further characterized using trajectory and pseudotime analysis.
Trajectory inference was performed using Slingshot 34 .
text.formatted: Trajectory inference was performed using Slingshot <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: The trajectory was rooted in the immature/banded cluster, based on its high ribosomal gene content, indicating a less mature neutrophil state.
Pseudotime values were extracted separately for each lineage.
Cells not assigned to a given lineage received no pseudotime value for that lineage and were excluded from the corresponding analysis.
To visualize gene expression dynamics along each trajectory, the top four marker genes per cluster were identified.

For each gene and each lineage, expression (SCT-normalized) was fitted against pseudotime using local polynomial regression (loess, span=0.3) across 200 evenly spaced points spanning that lineage's pseudotime range.
The smoothed values were z-scored per gene within each lineage.

To test whether this lineage bias was already detectable within the immature cluster itself, composite module scores representing the interferon-stimulated and aged transcriptional programs were computed.

These were derived from genes differentially expressed between these two clusters (FindMarkers, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, log2 fold-change threshold 0.25, adjusted p<0.05), with genes enriched in each cluster scored separately (AddModuleScore).

text.text: In brief, guidewires were cut into ±5 cm segments and transported on ice in complete endothelial cell medium.
To release adherent endothelial cells, the segments were rotated for 10 minutes at 4°C, after which the segments were removed from the medium.
Cells were pelleted by centrifugation, resuspended in complete endothelial cell medium and seeded onto a gelatin-coated 12-well plate.
Cultures were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2 with medium refreshed three times weekly.
At passage 2, endothelial cells were harvested for bulk RNA sequencing, which was performed as described previously 24.

To test the hypothesis that women with a low CFR have more activated neutrophils compared to women with a normal CFR, we tested neutrophil surface marker expression.

Both neutrophils isolated from systemic blood at baseline and after ex vivo stimulation with fNLF were characterized.

To investigate whether CFR-associated transcriptional changes were specific to particular neutrophil clusters, we performed cluster-specific pseudobulk differential expression analyses, modelling CFR as a continuous variable.
We did not observe significant differentially expressed genes in the mature, the IFN-activated, or aged neutrophil clusters.
In contrast, the immature cluster exhibited a distinct transcriptional signature associated with CFR.

Within the immature neutrophils, transcriptional profiles were leaning towards an IFN-activated (relative to an aged) phenotype in patients with a lower CFR (p=0.024, mixed-effects model accounting for multiple cells per patient) (Figure 4C, Supplemental Table S15), suggesting that immature neutrophils in patients with lower CFR are already transcriptionally primed towards an IFN-activated state.

text.text: These findings suggest that a lower CD62L MFI is associated with a shift in endothelial gene expression, characterized by reduced expression of genes and pathways characteristic of an immune-competent, quiescent endothelial phenotype and increased expression of proliferative and metabolic genes.
In this study, we characterized the circulating neutrophil phenotype in women with CMD and lower CFR using multiple complementary approaches.
Women with coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) and lower coronary flow reserve (CFR) showed a distinct circulating neutrophil phenotype.

Lower CFR was associated with higher neutrophil counts and inflammatory indices (NLR, SII), more activated CD62L dim neutrophils, and a larger interferon (IFN)-activated neutrophil cluster identified by single-cell RNA sequencing.

Immature neutrophils from these patients had reduced ribosomal and translational gene expression and were already skewed toward the IFN-activated profile, which may point to altered neutrophil maturation.

In patient-derived endothelial cells, lower CD62L expression on circulating neutrophils was linked to a shift from an immune-supportive state toward greater proliferative and metabolic activity, suggesting these neutrophils may affect endothelial biology.
The pathophysiology of CMD remains incompletely understood.

Previous studies on microvascular diseases have primarily focused on circulating neutrophil counts and NETosis 18, 19, 35, 43 , providing limited insight into neutrophil activation and transcriptional heterogeneity.
text.formatted: Previous studies on microvascular diseases have primarily focused on circulating neutrophil counts and NETosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> , providing limited insight into neutrophil activation and transcriptional heterogeneity.

text.text: By combining complete blood counts, flow cytometric activation phenotyping and single-cell transcriptomics, our study provides a multidimensional characterization of circulating neutrophils in relation to CMD.

Importantly, these analyses were performed in a well-phenotyped clinical cohort with invasively measured CFR, enabling assessment of the relationship between neutrophil phenotype and an objective, quantitative measure of coronary microvascular function.
The female predominance of CMD raises the question whether sex-specific immune biology contributes to the neutrophil phenotype observed in our study.
Indeed, neutrophils from healthy young women show stronger type I IFN signatures than those from men, despite similar circulating IFN activity and IFN receptor expression.
This difference appears to reflect enhanced intracellular signaling, including greater nuclear localization of IFN-responsive transcription factors, rather than greater IFN exposure.
The female-biased response was linked to estrogen and was absent before puberty, suggesting that sex hormones may shape neutrophil responsiveness 44 .
text.formatted: The female-biased response was linked to estrogen and was absent before puberty, suggesting that sex hormones may shape neutrophil responsiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> .

text.text: Complementing these observations, a recent singlecell atlas of human neutrophils identified a higher proportion of neutrophils expressing combined type I and II IFN-associated programs in healthy female donors 33 .
text.formatted: Complementing these observations, a recent singlecell atlas of human neutrophils identified a higher proportion of neutrophils expressing combined type I and II IFN-associated programs in healthy female donors <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: Together, these observations suggest that the neutrophil phenotype observed in our CMD cohort reflects, in part, an amplification of pre-existing sex differences in neutrophil IFN responsiveness.

Related evidence of sex-specific IFN-associated pathways in cardiovascular disease, including heart failure with preserved ejection fraction 45 and other female-predominant conditions 46, 47 , further supports the potential relevance of sex-dependent IFN signaling in shaping immune phenotypes and contributing to disease susceptibility.

text.text: This raises the possibility that these differences precede clinical disease, although longitudinal studies are needed to establish their contribution to CMD.
Importantly, our findings suggest that this IFN-biased phenotype may emerge already early in neutrophil maturation.
Our pseudotime analysis indicated that immature neutrophils from patients with lower CFR were already transcriptionally skewed towards an IFN-activated state.
Consistent with this, the association between CD62L dim neutrophils and CFR observed at baseline was no longer evident following ex vivo fNLF stimulation.

Although stimulation may alter CD62L surface expression and obscure baseline differences, this finding suggests that lower CFR is associated with a pre-existing neutrophil state that is not simply explained by an enhanced acute response to stimulation.
Endothelial dysfunction contributes to impaired coronary microvascular regulation in CMD 3 .
text.formatted: Endothelial dysfunction contributes to impaired coronary microvascular regulation in CMD <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The proportion of IFN-activated neutrophils identified in our study was associated with a reduced surface CD62L, pointing to altered neutrophil-endothelial interactions.
CD62L mediates initial neutrophil rolling, and its shedding accompanies activation and the transition to firm adhesion 39 .
text.formatted: CD62L mediates initial neutrophil rolling, and its shedding accompanies activation and the transition to firm adhesion <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> .

text.text: Despite lower surface CD62L, SELL transcript expression was higher with increasing proportions of IFN-activated neutrophils, potentially reflecting ongoing transcription alongside protein shedding.
However, our data cannot establish whether shedding is ongoing or whether these neutrophils interact directly with the endothelium.

In our endothelial cell data, we found that lower neutrophil CD62L MFI was associated with increased endothelial proliferative and metabolic activity, consistent with a shift away from a quiescent state.

This may be consistent with evidence that type I IFN signaling can promote endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment, reduce nitric oxide bioavailability, impair endothelial repair and promote NET formation and thrombosis [48] [49] [50] .
text.formatted: This may be consistent with evidence that type I IFN signaling can promote endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment, reduce nitric oxide bioavailability, impair endothelial repair and promote NET formation and thrombosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[48]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[49]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[50]</ref> .

text.text: IFN-activated neutrophils may therefore influence endothelial function through altered adhesion or inflammatory signaling, potentially contributing to microvascular dysfunction.

However, the direction of this relationship remains unclear: the neutrophil phenotype may contribute to endothelial dysfunction, arise in response to pre-existing abnormalities, or reflect a shared underlying process.

These findings raise the possibility that IFN-associated neutrophil activation may be a therapeutic target in CMD, although further functional studies are needed to establish its causal role and therapeutic relevance.
Future work should build on our associative findings in several directions.
Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether this neutrophil phenotype precedes the development of CMD or arises as a consequence of reduced CFR.
Some of our data suggests that, at least in part, this phenotype might be encoded already in immature neutrophil stages.
Functional studies are needed to establish whether CD62L shedding and the IFN-activated neutrophil phenotype causally affect neutrophil-endothelial adhesion and coronary microvascular function.

In addition, the higher CXCR1 and CXCR2 expression in immature neutrophils from patients with a lower CFR, together with our parallel observation of elevated plasma CXCL6 in patients with a lower CFR, suggests a candidate signaling axis that merits further mechanistic investigation (Kregting, BHCM et al., unpublished data, 2026).
It also remains unclear whether this circulating phenotype preferentially affects the coronary microcirculation or instead, reflects a more generalized marker of systemic microvascular vulnerability.
Examining whether specific features of the coronary endothelium, or its hemodynamic environment confer susceptibility, would help clarify this.

Finally, direct measurements of circulating IFN levels and sex-hormones would allow the proposed estrogen-driven mechanism of neutrophil IFN predisposition to be tested directly, rather than inferred from prior literature in healthy cohorts.
This study has several limitations.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about causality, as discussed above.
Second, this was a single-center study, which may limit generalizability.
Third, the number of men included for single-cell RNA sequencing and the supplementary subgroup analyses was small, limiting statistical power for these analyses.
In conclusion, this study provides the first detailed phenotypic characterization of circulating neutrophils in patients with CMD.

We identified a circulating neutrophil phenotype marked by an increase in IFN-activated neutrophils, an IFN-enriched immature neutrophil phenotype and CD62L shedding, with potential relevance to coronary endothelial function.

These findings provide pathophysiological insight into a condition that disproportionately affects women, positioning neutrophil activation as a candidate contributor to CMD and underscoring the importance of sex-specific research in cardiovascular disease.
